question: How much more reward is there for praying in Masjid al-Aqsa?
answer:
We are all aware that when we pray in the Haram in Makkah, we get 100,000 times reward, and when we pray in the Masjid of Medina, we get 1,000 times reward extra. What is the blessing for praying in Masjid al-Aqsa, for praying in this location? So there are a number of traditions in this regard, and unfortunately, all of them have disputes about how authentic they are.

So we have one group of traditions. For example, al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam narrated, and it is reported in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad and other books of hadith, that our Prophet ﷺ said that the salah in Makkah is better than a thousand prayers compared to Bayt al-Maqdis. The salah in Makkah is better than a thousand prayers compared to Bayt al-Maqdis. So a thousand times a thousand gives you a hundred thousand. So according to this understanding, praying in Bayt al-Maqdis would be around a thousand times. That is one opinion that has been derived.

Another opinion is that the salah in Masjid al-Aqsa is worth 500 of the prayers outside of Masjid al-Aqsa, and that is mentioned in a hadith in the Musnad of al-Bazzar and others: that whoever prays a salah in the Masjid of al-Aqsa, it will be 500 salah; it is going to be equal to 500 prayers. So we have the ratio of one to 500. So Masjid al-Aqsa becomes 500.

And then we have one tradition, which is in the Mustadrak of al-Hakim and the Sunan of ad-Daraqutni, from Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, that our Prophet ﷺ said that the prayer in my masjid is better than four prayers in Masjid Bayt al-Maqdis, in Masjid al-Aqsa. So this gives us the ratio of 1 to 250: 250 times.

Now we therefore have three numbers: 1,000, 500 and 250. By the way, there is a tradition that is considered fabricated or rejected, in which it says that one salah is equal to 50,000 salawat, and that is considered to be absolutely not authentic. However, these three ahadith, 1,000, 500 and 250, are all similar in terms of credibility.

And this has led to a lot of discussion. Some people say that firstly the Prophet said 250, then he upgraded it to 500, then he upgraded it to 1,000. So according to this opinion, the prayer in Masjid al-Aqsa and the prayer in Medina are the same. That is one opinion, and perhaps Shaykh al-Albani and others kind of leaned towards that position towards the end of their lives. Other groups of scholars say that it depends on the khushu' of the person praying: if it's low khushu', it's 250; if it's high khushu', it's going to be 500 or 1,000. This is another opinion. And Ibn al-Qayyim famously remarked that the strongest hadith is the 500 one. So he said that praying in Masjid al-Aqsa is worth 500 salawat compared to anywhere else.

At the end of the day, dear sister, and all of us that are watching, **the technicalities of how many more is really not the important point. The point is that it is a blessed place, and it is a place that we should travel to.**

And of course, the most authentic hadith about the blessings of Masjid al-Aqsa is the famous hadith of Abu Hurayrah radiyallahu 'anhu, reported in Bukhari and in Muslim, that our Prophet ﷺ said, "La tushaddu al-rihal": that the camel is not made ready and prepared to travel except to one of three locations: Masjid al-Haram, and my Masjid here in Medina, and Masjid al-Aqsa.

The meaning of this hadith is very clear, and that is that there is no region on earth that is considered to be extra blessed to worship Allah in, other than these three regions. You should not make what we call in English a pilgrimage. When I say pilgrimage, I don't mean the Hajj. A pilgrimage is a holy journey; a pilgrimage is a journey that you go on to get blessings. Now, we may travel for sightseeing, we may travel for business, we may travel for knowledge, we may travel to get married, we may travel for a billion reasons on earth. But to travel thinking that the destination you're going to is holier than where you are at: there are only three places. There are only three places on earth that are inherently blessed, and that's what our Prophet ﷺ is saying.

I am living currently in Dallas, Texas. There is no mosque anywhere on earth that is worthy for me to travel to just for the sake of praying there. I can travel to meet a friend, I can travel to give a lecture, but to think that, oh, there is a masjid in, let's say, Cincinnati or in Timbuktu, whatever it is, and that masjid is worthy for me to spend my time and money and to travel there: there is no such place on earth. There are only three holy lands, three blessed places, that inherently to go there simply for the sake of making du'a and making extra dhikr and reading the Qur'an and giving charity and praying to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala; only three places are extra holy. And these are obviously Mecca and Medina and Jerusalem. So this is what this hadith means: that there are three inherently holy places on earth.
